content: BIN1, also referred to as Bridging Integrator-1 or Amphiphysin-2, is a protein encoded by the BIN1 gene in humans. This gene produces multiple isoforms of a nucleocytoplasmic adaptor protein. One of these isoforms was initially identified as a MYC-interacting protein with characteristics of a tumor suppressor. Isoforms of BIN1 expressed in the central nervous system are thought to play a role in synaptic vesicle endocytosis. These isoforms may interact with proteins such as dynamin, synaptojanin, endophilin, and clathrin. In contrast, isoforms expressed in muscle tissue and ubiquitously expressed isoforms are localized to the cytoplasm and nucleus, where they can activate a caspase-independent apoptotic pathway. Research in mice suggests that the BIN1 gene is critical for the development of cardiac muscle. Alternative splicing of the BIN1 gene results in the production of ten transcript variants, each encoding different isoforms. Additionally, aberrant splice variants of BIN1 have been identified in tumor cell lines. Clinical Significance In humans, mutations in the BIN1 gene have been linked to skeletal myopathies, including centronuclear myopathy, which causes muscle weakness, and myotonic dystrophy, which leads to progressive muscle wasting, myotonia, cataracts, and defects in cardiac conduction. Furthermore, BIN1 mutations have been associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease. Knockdown of BIN1 in zebrafish results in a cardiomyopathy phenotype. In sheep, BIN1 may contribute to the loss of T-tubules observed in heart failure. Interactions BIN1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including Phospholipase D1 (PLD1), Sorting Nexin 4 (SNX4), and Phospholipase D2 (PLD2).
